title: Open-weight text-diffusion LLMs add a second family or edge runtime by Q1 2027
body: Google's June 10 release of DiffusionGemma under Apache 2.0 is the moment open-weight text diffusion stopped being a research curiosity and shipped as a usable local model: a 26B Mixture-of-Experts (3.8B active) built on the Gemma 4 backbone with an added diffusion head, it abandons left-to-right autoregressive decoding to refine a 256-token block in parallel over multiple passes, locking in confident tokens as context for up to 4x faster generation, and it lands with native support across vLLM, Hugging Face Transformers, MLX, NVIDIA NeMo, and Unsloth, plus a shipped Unsloth Sudoku fine-tune that exploits its bidirectional attention. Two things make this a seed rather than a one-off. First, Google is explicit that output quality trails standard autoregressive Gemma 4 and steers production work back to the autoregressive model, positioning diffusion squarely for speed-critical, low-concurrency local inference - the exact envelope an edge runtime is built to fill. Second, the on-device stack is not yet ready for it: llama.cpp support is listed only as coming, so the GGUF/CPU path where Gemma-class weights are actually deployed locally cannot run block-parallel diffusion decoding on launch day, and the open-weight text-diffusion field has exactly one member. The forward thesis is that text diffusion hardens into an established open-weight model category rather than remaining a single Google checkpoint. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q1 2027 EITHER a second independent major open-weight text-diffusion language model ships with its own model card and weights under a permissive or open license from a non-Google publisher (the strongest candidates being Alibaba/Qwen, Meta, DeepSeek, Mistral, or NVIDIA), OR a mainstream on-device inference runtime that did not support it at DiffusionGemma's launch - llama.cpp foremost, or LM Studio, Ollama, or MLX as a packaged GGUF/edge path - ships first-class block-parallel text-diffusion decoding so the format runs on the consumer CPU/edge stack. A research-only paper with no released weights, a one-off Google follow-up checkpoint, or a runtime that merely wraps the existing PyTorch path without native diffusion-decoding support does not count; the marker is a second independent open-weight diffusion-LLM release or genuine edge-runtime support for the decoding scheme. If by March 31, 2027 DiffusionGemma is still the only open-weight text-diffusion model and no mainstream on-device runtime has added native diffusion decoding, the prediction fails.

reasoning.because: DiffusionGemma shipped June 10 as the first open-weight text-diffusion LLM; no llama.cpp support yet
reasoning.given: diffusion's 4x-faster low-concurrency profile fits the edge, but the GGUF/CPU stack can't run it yet
reasoning.so_that: a second open-weight diffusion LLM ships, or a mainstream on-device runtime adds native diffusion decoding
reasoning.landing: by Q1 2027: a second open-weight diffusion LLM, or on-device diffusion decoding
reasoning.plain_language: Google made the first open AI that writes in parallel, not word by word; soon a rival copies it or local apps run it.

summary: The June 10 DiffusionGemma is the first major open-weight text-diffusion LLM, decoding 256-token blocks in parallel for up to 4x faster output, but llama.cpp support is only coming. Expect text diffusion to form an open-weight category by Q1 2027 via a second release or on-device runtime support.
